prompt: Panela doubles its sign-ups and '% of customers who ordered this month' rises, though nobody's behaviour changed. Why?

choices.text: New customers order more often
choices.why: The premise is that nobody's behaviour changed.

choices.text: More customers are new, and new ones have not had time to leave
choices.why: Right. The average mixes loyalty with when people joined.

choices.text: A seasonal effect
choices.why: Seasons were not mentioned; the mix of ages was.

choices.text: The calculation divides by the wrong month
choices.why: The arithmetic is right; the population changed.

choices.text: A shared start
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Customers with the same number of orders
choices.why: That groups by the behaviour being measured.

choices.text: The customers active this month, whatever month each of them first signed up in
choices.why: That is a snapshot, the thing cohorts replace.

choices.text: A region, such as the North or the Southeast
choices.why: A region can cut a cohort, but it is not a starting event.

choices.text: Staying long is how you get ten orders, so the result is built in

prompt: A delivery outage in March 2025 lowered orders for every customer that month. Where does it show in the cohort table?

choices.text: Along a diagonal
choices.why: Right. Cells on a diagonal share a calendar month.

choices.text: In the March 2025 row only

choices.text: Nowhere, since cohorts remove calendar effects, which is why they are used

choices.text: Otherwise the small cohort moves the average as much as the large one
choices.why: Right. Unweighted, it reads 75%; weighted, about 62%.
